passages.t: Sour grapes: each person answers to God
passages.happening:
The people quote a proverb: ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge’ (verse 2). God forbids it. ‘Behold, every soul belongs to Me; both father and son are Mine. The soul who sins is the one who will die’ (verse 4).

Then come three generations. A righteous man keeps God's ways: he does not worship idols or defile his neighbor's wife, he returns a poor man's pledge, gives bread to the hungry and clothes the naked, takes no interest and judges fairly. ‘That man is righteous; surely he will live’ (verse 9). If his son is violent and does none of these things, the son will die for his own sins (verses 10-13). If that son's son sees his father's sins and does not copy them, he will live (verses 14-17).

‘The soul who sins is the one who will die. A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The proverb was common talk. Jeremiah quotes it too. The generation that saw Judah's collapse had been told for decades that King Manasseh's sins had sealed its fate, and that teaching had turned into a slogan: the fathers sinned, the children pay, and nothing they do can change it.

The portrait of the righteous man is a short summary of Israel's law, the kind a priest knew by heart. Much of it is about the poor. A creditor who took a poor man's cloak as a pledge had to return it by sunset so that he could sleep in it, and Israelites were forbidden to charge interest to a neighbor in need. Worship, faithfulness in marriage and mercy with money stand side by side as one obedience.
passages.later: The law already said, ‘each is to die for his own sin’ (Deuteronomy 24:16). Jeremiah promised a day when the sour-grapes proverb would no longer be said (Jeremiah 31:29-30).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter contradict the warning that God visits the iniquity of fathers on children?

The Ten Commandments speak of God visiting the iniquity of fathers on children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate him, while Ezekiel says a son will not bear his father's iniquity. Readers have handled the tension in several ways. Many note that the commandment itself speaks of those who hate God, children who carry on their parents' sin, which is the very case of Ezekiel's violent son. Others point out that the law already forbade courts to punish children for their parents' crimes, and see Ezekiel applying that to God's own dealings. Others see a real development in Scripture, from a strong sense that families and nations stand or fall together toward a sharper stress on each person.

Ezekiel is not writing a full theory of justice. He is answering a specific despair, and his word is pastoral: your parents' history does not close your door. The siege still fell on everyone in Jerusalem; what the chapter denies is that anyone stands condemned before God for a guilt that is not their own.

Nor does the chapter teach that every hardship is a punishment the sufferer deserved. It is a call to turn, not a way of explaining anyone's pain, and it gives no one the right to read another person's suffering that way. Jesus refused that reasoning about a man born blind (John 9:2-3).
passages.asks: The exiles thought their parents' sins had sealed their fate. Ask what you have inherited that you thought you could never escape. And ask what it means that God says your story is not closed.

passages.happening:
‘But if the wicked man turns from all the sins he has committed, keeps all My statutes, and does what is just and right, he will surely live; he will not die’ (verse 21). His past sins will not be held against him (verse 22). ‘Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?’ (verse 23). But a righteous person who turns to evil will die in his sin (verse 24).

The people say, ‘The way of the Lord is not just’ (verse 25). God answers that it is their ways that are unjust (verses 25-29). ‘Repent and turn from all your transgressions’ (verse 30). ‘Cast away from yourselves all the transgressions you have committed, and fashion for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why should you die, O house of Israel?’ (verse 31). “For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death, declares the Lord GOD. So repent and live!” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The chapter argues like a court case. It quotes what the people are saying, then answers it. The word turn, shuv in Hebrew, runs through the second half and becomes the closing command.

God tells the people to make themselves a new heart and a new spirit. Later in the book he promises to give them exactly that (36:26-27). The command shows the need; the promise meets it.

The people's complaint, that God is unfair, is turned back on them twice. A God who welcomes the one who turns is not unjust.
passages.later: God later promises, ‘I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you’ (Ezekiel 36:26). Moses set the same choice before Israel: ‘Therefore choose life’ (Deuteronomy 30:19).
passages.asks: God takes no pleasure in anyone's death. Ask what you need to turn from today. And ask whether you believe that he wants you to live.
